## Original idea
{
  "title": "Disentangling Competing Calibration Biases via Geometry-Aware Activation Steering",
  "core_problem": "LLM miscalibration arises from at least two competing biases — choice-supportive bias (CSB, inflating confidence in initial answers) and contradictory-evidence overweighting (CEO, causing excessive confidence revision under criticism) — that require opposing corrections. Existing calibration methods apply uniform corrections that cannot simultaneously address biases pulling confidence in opposite directions. Recent work reveals two deeper obstacles. First, a classification-correction gap (Liu, 2605.05715): failure-mode directions that are linearly decodable may not be linearly steerable due to entanglement with task-critical computation (specificity ratio ≤0.152), meaning that even if competing biases can be identified in activations, correcting them requires knowing not just WHICH bias dominates but WHETHER each bias direction is steerable. Second, even principled adaptive frameworks like MERA (Hedström et al., ICML 2025) that optimize intervention strength and abstain when correction is unsafe still treat errors monolithically — they cannot decompose miscalibration into opposing sources or route different bias types to different intervention strategies. The rapidly maturing nonlinear steering landscape (ODESteer, ICLR 2026; Curveball Steering, 2026; FLAS, 2026) provides powerful general-purpose alternatives to linear steering, yet none address the diagnosis problem: which competing bias dominates per-instance, and what is its steerability profile? Can we jointly diagnose per-instance bias dominance AND steerability to apply targeted, manifold-preserving corrections where possible and graceful degradation where not?",
  "opportunity": "Kumaran et al. (Nature Machine Intelligence, 2026; arXiv 2507.03120) identified that LLM miscalibration results from two mechanistically distinct behavioral biases in Gemma 3, GPT-4o, and o1-preview: choice-supportive bias inflates confidence in selected answers, while contradictory-advice overweighting causes models to over-react to opposing evidence. Miao & Ungar (arXiv 2603.25052, 2026) independently showed that calibration and verbalized confidence signals are encoded linearly but orthogonally in the residual stream across three 7-8B models, establishing that confidence-related constructs have accessible geometric structure. Liu (arXiv 2605.05715, May 2026) demonstrated a critical classification-correction gap: linearly decodable failure directions (71.6% balanced accuracy) yield Δ≈0 under 29 steering configurations because the failure directions have 85-88% overlap with task-critical computation — but crucially, a learned non-linear residual MLP achieves Δ=+2.8pp where all linear methods fail, and the decodable signal still supports selective abstention (AUROC 0.610). Hedström et al. (MERA, ICML 2025; arXiv 2510.13290) established that steering benefits from principled adaptive strength calibration and provable non-degradation guarantees via constrained optimization (min ‖v‖² s.t. p̂(h+v) ≤ α) — but MERA's monolithic error probe cannot distinguish between calibration errors arising from opposing bias sources. Meanwhile, the nonlinear steering landscape has rapidly matured: ODESteer (Chen et al., ICLR 2026; arXiv 2602.17560) unified existing methods under a barrier-function ODE framework with multi-step adaptive steering; Curveball Steering (Raval et al., arXiv 2603.09313, Mar 2026) introduced polynomial kernel PCA to respect curved activation geometry; and FLAS (arXiv 2605.05892, May 2026) learned concept-conditioned velocity fields that first outperformed prompting on AxBench. The 'Confidence Manifold' study (arXiv 2602.08159) found correctness signals occupy only 3-8 dimensions with simple mean-shift geometry across 9 models, suggesting that calibration-related directions may have more favorable specificity profiles than entangled failure modes. The convergence of (a) identified competing biases, (b) linear confidence encoding evidence, (c) the decodable-steerable distinction with quantitative diagnostics, (d) both norm-preserving rotation (Spherical Steering, ICML 2026) and adaptive frameworks (MERA), (e) nonlinear steering alternatives for when linear methods fail, and (f) collateral-damage-aware optimization (COAST, 2605.01167) creates an opportunity for a principled pipeline: decompose calibration error into competing biases, assess per-direction steerability, and route to the appropriate intervention — extending MERA's adaptive principle from monolithic to bias-specific.",
  "landscape": "Kumaran et al. (Nature MI, 2026) identified competing biases (CSB and CEO) via behavioral experiments on Gemma 3, GPT-4o, and o1-preview but proposed no correction framework and provided no mechanistic (activation-level) evidence. Miao & Ungar (arXiv 2603.25052, 2026) demonstrated that calibration accuracy and verbalized confidence are linearly encoded but orthogonal in 7-8B models (cosine similarity <0.04 across layers), and introduced adaptive steering achieving 4-7× ECE improvement — but they target the confidence-accuracy misalignment gap, not the competing bias structure. Tsujimura & Tagade (arXiv 2508.17182, Aug 2025) decomposed LLM assertiveness into emotional and logical sub-components via unsupervised clustering on Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (645 samples), finding two clusters in high-assertive representations — methodologically adjacent but critically different: their decomposition is descriptive (post-hoc ChatGPT-labeled clusters) rather than causally grounded in identified cognitive biases, uses a single 1B model, reports no calibration metrics, and addresses assertiveness rather than calibration. The 'Wired for Overconfidence' paper (2604.01457, April 2026) identifies overconfidence circuits in Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B, achieving 96.9% ECE reduction on PopQA via monolithic activation steering, but only tests 3B models and treats overconfidence as a single phenomenon.

Liu (arXiv 2605.05715, May 2026) is the most directly relevant advance on the decodable-steerable gap: linearly decodable failure directions (71.6% balanced accuracy on Llama-3.1-8B) yield Δ≈0 across five families of linear steering (29 configurations) because the failure direction has 85-88% overlap with task-critical computation (specificity ratio ≤0.152). Three convergent evidence lines confirm entanglement: low specificity, shared-direction steering damages accuracy (-12.1pp), and LEACE concept erasure damages accuracy (-3.6pp). A learned non-linear bottleneck MLP (4096→64→4096) achieves Δ=+2.8pp (p=0.025) where linear methods fail, and selective abstention outperforms 5 uncertainty baselines (AUROC 0.610). However, this was studied for medical overthinking, a single failure mode.

Hedström et al. (MERA, ICML 2025; arXiv 2510.13290) established the most principled framework for selective steering to date: MERA solves a constrained optimization problem (min ‖v‖² s.t. p̂(h+v) ≤ α) to derive per-instance adaptive steering strength, and calibrates the intervention threshold α* with provable non-degradation guarantees via Hoeffding bounds with Bonferroni correction — either finding a statistically significant improvement or abstaining. MERA can be applied on top of existing steering methods. However, MERA operates with a single monolithic error probe and a single linear steering direction; it cannot decompose calibration errors into opposing sources (CSB vs. CEO) or route to different intervention types based on per-direction steerability assessment. MERA also acknowledges its inherently linear intervention as a limitation.

The nonlinear steering landscape has matured rapidly. ODESteer (Chen et al., ICLR 2026; arXiv 2602.17560) formulated a unified ODE-based framework where identifying a steering direction is equivalent to designing a barrier function from control theory, enabling multi-step adaptive steering via numerical ODE solvers — achieving consistent improvements on TruthfulQA, UltraFeedback, and RealToxicityPrompts across Falcon-7B, Mistral-7B, LLaMA3.1-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B. Curveball Steering (Raval et al., arXiv 2603.09313, Mar 2026) used polynomial kernel PCA to perform interventions in a curved feature space rather than globally linear directions, demonstrating up to +47% improvement over linear steering in high-curvature regimes (κ>8) on Llama-3.2-1B and Phi-3.5-mini — but is tested only on behavioral attributes (power-seeking, corrigibility), not calibration. FLAS (arXiv 2605.05892, May 2026) learned a concept-conditioned velocity field via flow matching, becoming the first steering method to consistently outperform prompting on AxBench (harmonic mean 1.015-1.113), with a 97.6-255M parameter FlowBlock — a powerful but heavy general-purpose approach. These nonlinear methods address the geometric limitations of linear steering but do not provide bias decomposition or steerability-based routing.

Ji et al. (EMNLP 2025) modulates a single Verbal Uncertainty Feature direction, reducing hallucinations by ~30%, capturing only the net effect of competing biases. Joshi et al. (EMNLP 2025) found a single calibration direction but did not decompose it. CORAL (arXiv 2602.06022, Feb 2026) achieves 49% ECE improvement via correctness-subspace probing on 7B models but uses a single MLP probe direction. The 'Confidence Manifold' study (arXiv 2602.08159, Feb 2026) found correctness signals occupy 3-8 dimensions with simple mean-shift geometry across 9 models from 5 families, and causally validated via steering (10.9pp error rate change) — the low dimensionality and linear separability contrasts with Liu's high-entanglement finding for overthinking, suggesting calibration-related directions may have more favorable specificity profiles. Wang & Stengel-Eskin (ICLR 2026) introduced DINCO to normalize suggestibility bias via self-generated distractors at the output level. Zhuang et al. (arXiv 2025) proposed RDG to alleviate choice-supportive bias through fine-tuning but did not address CEO. 'Breaking the Mirror' (arXiv 2509.03647) found that self-preference bias 'spans multiple or nonlinear directions,' achieving 97% unjustified bias reduction but with instability on legitimate cases.

On the steering methodology side: Spherical Steering (arXiv 2602.08169, ICML 2026) performs norm-preserving geodesic rotation, outperforming addition-based baselines by +10% on TruthfulQA. Selective Steering (Dang & Ngo, arXiv 2601.19375, Jan 2026) independently developed norm-preserving rotation with discriminative layer selection, achieving 5.5× higher attack success rates with zero perplexity violations across 8 models. COAST (Nguyen et al., arXiv 2605.01167, May 2026) formalizes collateral damage from steering as unintended alignment changes along non-target feature directions, achieving up to 30% improvement over Angular Steering. AUSteer (arXiv 2602.04428) decomposes block activations into fine-grained atomic units. CLAS (arXiv 2604.24693) dynamically adapts steering strengths per-context. 'Steered LLM Activations are Non-Surjective' (2604.09839) formally proved that additive steering pushes activations off-manifold.

No existing method jointly decomposes calibration error into competing biases, assesses the steerability of each bias direction, and routes to bias-specific interventions. MERA provides adaptive strength and abstention but is monolithic and linear; the nonlinear methods (ODESteer, Curveball, FLAS) provide powerful alternatives to linear steering but lack bias decomposition and steerability diagnosis. DBS-v2 fills this gap by combining bias-grounded decomposition with steerability-aware routing, using MERA's adaptive framework as a building block for steerable directions and Liu's nonlinear MLP for entangled ones.",
  "inspired_by": "Gap: Competing biases create non-uniform miscalibration patterns that even adaptive monolithic methods like MERA cannot optimally correct (Kumaran et al. 2026), while the classification-correction gap (Liu, 2605.05715) shows that decodable directions are not necessarily steerable. Pattern: Theory-driven contrastive probing (Miao & Ungar 2026) + steerability diagnostics (specificity ratio, Liu 2026) + adaptive intervention with non-degradation guarantees (MERA, ICML 2025) + nonlinear fallback when linear fails (Liu's MLP finding, supported by the broader nonlinear landscape of ODESteer/Curveball/FLAS). Untried combination: Cognitive-bias-grounded contrastive stimuli → per-instance bias diagnosis → specificity-informed intervention routing (MERA-wrapped Spherical Steering for steerable directions / lightweight nonlinear MLP for entangled directions / statistical abstention), with the hypothesis that CSB and CEO may have asymmetric steerability profiles.",
  "approach": "We design DBS-v2 (Disentangled Bias Steering) in three phases, incorporating the critical decodable-steerable distinction (Liu, 2605.05715) and streamlined to a focused experimental matrix of 3 models × 3 datasets × 3 intervention routes.

**Phase 1 — Assumption Validation & Steerability Assessment (Weeks 1-5):**

*Phase 1A — Separability (Weeks 1-3):* We construct two contrastive stimulus sets: for CSB, we compare hidden states when the model reviews its own prior answer vs. a fresh unattributed answer (eliciting choice-supportive inflation); for CEO, we compare states when contradictory expert advice is present vs. absent (eliciting evidence overweighting). Using difference-in-means on these contrastive pairs, we extract candidate bias directions in the residual stream. We validate separability via: (a) cosine similarity between candidate directions, (b) principal angle analysis between CSB and CEO subspaces using the methodology of Miao & Ungar (2026), (c) PCA to assess whether 2 directions capture sufficient variance vs. requiring higher-dimensional subspaces, and (d) cross-prediction ablations to confirm removing one bias subspace does not collapse the other. If CSB and CEO directions show cosine similarity >0.3 or shared variance >15%, we activate the separability fallback: extracting a multi-direction bias subspace via SAE-derived features and training a subspace projection classifier.

*Phase 1B — Steerability Diagnostics (Weeks 3-5):* Even if CSB and CEO are separable, steering along identified directions may fail if those directions are entangled with task-critical computation. For each identified bias direction, we compute: (a) the **specificity ratio** — the proportion of mode-specific variance vs. shared variance with the correct-vs-incorrect subspace, following Liu's shared-specific decomposition methodology; (b) **LEACE concept erasure test** — applying concept erasure to each bias direction and measuring accuracy damage as causal evidence of entanglement; (c) **pilot linear steering test** — applying small-magnitude Spherical Steering along each direction and measuring both calibration improvement and accuracy impact.

Critically, we do NOT pre-commit to fixed routing thresholds. The specificity ratio boundaries proposed by Liu (≤0.152 for overthinking where linear fails; ~0.999 for refusal where linear succeeds) provide initial reference points, but the actual relationship between specificity and steering effectiveness for calibration biases is an open empirical question. We instead LEARN the routing thresholds by sweeping specificity cutoffs on a held-out validation set and reporting the full specificity-vs-effectiveness curve as a primary empirical contribution. We hypothesize that CSB and CEO may have asymmetric specificity profiles — one may be more steerable than the other — which would provide a mechanistic explanation for why monolithic calibration steering sometimes succeeds partially.

Phase 1 results constitute an independent contribution: the first joint separability-and-steerability assessment of behaviorally-identified competing biases, providing the field's first specificity ratio measurements for calibration-related bias directions.

**Phase 2 — Per-Instance Bias Diagnosis (Weeks 4-7):** A lightweight logistic probe (or, in the fallback case, a small MLP) trained on per-instance projection magnitudes onto each bias direction classifies which bias dominates for a given query. We stratify by difficulty: on easy questions where models are already confident, CSB likely dominates; on hard questions under criticism, CEO likely dominates. The probe output provides a continuous dominance score. The Phase 1B steerability assessment informs a per-direction intervention routing table, so the probe determines both which bias is active and which intervention to apply.

**Phase 3 — Adaptive Intervention (Weeks 6-12):** Instead of a single intervention strategy, Phase 3 implements three intervention routes informed by Phase 1B's learned steerability thresholds:

*Route A — Adaptive Spherical Steering (for steerable directions):* When a bias direction has specificity above the learned threshold for effective linear intervention, we apply Spherical Steering (You et al., ICML 2026) with MERA-inspired adaptive strength: for each instance, the rotation magnitude is optimized to minimize ‖v‖² subject to the bias probe's predicted error falling below a calibrated threshold α*, following MERA's constrained optimization framework (Hedström et al., ICML 2025). This combines Spherical Steering's norm-preservation (addressing the off-manifold concern of Mishra et al., 2604.09839) with MERA's adaptive strength calibration and non-degradation guarantees. Unlike MERA applied monolithically, our adaptation operates per-bias-direction, allowing different strengths for CSB vs. CEO corrections.

*Route B — Learned Non-Linear Residual Correction (for entangled directions):* When a bias direction has specificity below the learned threshold, linear steering is expected to fail. Following Liu's finding that a bottleneck residual MLP (d→64→d) achieves Δ=+2.8pp where 29 linear configurations yield Δ≈0, we train a small non-linear residual adapter per bias type. We choose this lightweight architecture (< 0.1% of model parameters) over heavier nonlinear alternatives — Curveball Steering requires kernel PCA with pre-image reconstruction, FLAS requires a 97-255M parameter FlowBlock, ODESteer requires ODE solver iterations — because Liu's calibration-specific evidence directly validates the bottleneck MLP for the regime we target (entangled failure directions), and the minimal parameter footprint preserves inference efficiency. We incorporate COAST-informed training (Nguyen et al., 2605.01167) by weighting the loss by the empirical second-moment matrix to minimize expected collateral damage along non-target feature directions.

*Route C — Selective Abstention (for uncorrectable instances):* When neither Route A nor Route B improves calibration without excessive accuracy damage (> 3% degradation on validation), we leverage the decodable signal for selective abstention. Following MERA's statistical framework, we apply Hoeffding-based confidence bounds to determine whether any intervention yields statistically significant improvement; if not, we abstain and output a reliability score. This provides graceful degradation backed by MERA's provable non-degradation guarantees, extended to our bias-decomposed setting.

For intermediate-specificity directions, Route A is applied with a conservative strength cap (rotation magnitude ≤ 50% of high-specificity coefficient), falling back to Route C per-instance if collateral damage exceeds the threshold.

We evaluate on TriviaQA, MMLU, and PopQA across Gemma 4 31B (Dense), Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Metrics: ECE, Brier score, AUROC, difficulty-stratified ECE (easy/medium/hard partitions), per-direction specificity ratios, collateral damage measurements, and route-distribution analysis. Core baselines: (1) temperature scaling, (2) CORAL, (3) Miao & Ungar adaptive steering, (4) MERA applied monolithically (to isolate the contribution of bias decomposition over MERA's adaptive framework), (5) monolithic Spherical Steering (single direction, no bias decomposition), (6) monolithic non-linear residual MLP (single direction, no bias decomposition). Extended baselines in supplementary: CCPS, VUF intervention, DINCO, 'Wired for Overconfidence' replication at 3B scale.",

  "description": "We propose DBS-v2 (Disentangled Bias Steering), a method that separately identifies, assesses the steerability of, and adaptively corrects two competing sources of LLM miscalibration identified by Kumaran et al. (2026): choice-supportive bias (CSB) and contradictory-evidence overweighting (CEO).

A critical insight motivating this revision is that both monolithic steering (which cannot decompose competing biases) and uniform intervention strategies (which ignore the classification-correction gap) are fundamentally suboptimal. MERA (Hedström et al., ICML 2025) demonstrated that adaptive steering strength with abstention outperforms fixed steering — but MERA's single error probe cannot distinguish between opposing calibration biases. The nonlinear steering landscape (ODESteer, Curveball, FLAS) provides powerful geometry-aware alternatives — but none diagnose which bias dominates per-instance or assess per-direction steerability.

The method proceeds in three phases. Phase 1A (Separability Validation) tests whether CSB and CEO produce distinguishable activation signatures using contrastive activation probing, validated via cosine similarity, principal angle analysis, PCA dimensionality assessment, and cross-prediction ablation. Phase 1B (Steerability Assessment) computes the specificity ratio for each bias direction following Liu's (2605.05715) methodology, supplemented with LEACE concept erasure tests and pilot steering experiments. Rather than pre-committing to fixed routing thresholds (which would rest on only two empirical data points from Liu), we LEARN optimal thresholds via validation-set sweeps and report the full specificity-vs-effectiveness curve as a primary contribution. We hypothesize that CSB and CEO have asymmetric specificity profiles, explaining inconsistent monolithic steering results.

Phase 2 trains a lightweight per-instance bias dominance classifier. Phase 3 implements adaptive routing: (Route A) Spherical Steering with MERA-inspired adaptive strength optimization for steerable directions — combining norm-preservation with per-instance strength calibration and non-degradation guarantees, applied per-bias rather than monolithically; (Route B) a lightweight bottleneck residual MLP (d→64→d, <0.1% parameters) for entangled directions, chosen over heavier nonlinear alternatives (Curveball/FLAS/ODESteer) based on Liu's calibration-specific validation, trained with COAST-informed collateral-damage-aware loss; (Route C) selective abstention via MERA's statistical framework when neither route safely improves calibration.

We evaluate on TriviaQA, MMLU, and PopQA across Gemma 4 31B Dense, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Core baselines: temperature scaling, CORAL, Miao & Ungar adaptive steering, MERA (monolithic), monolithic Spherical Steering, and monolithic nonlinear MLP — isolating the contribution of bias decomposition from both the adaptive framework (vs. MERA) and the steering methodology (vs. monolithic variants). The primary contributions are: (1) the first joint separability-and-steerability assessment of competing calibration biases, with empirically-learned routing thresholds; (2) the hypothesis and test of asymmetric steerability profiles for CSB vs. CEO; (3) adaptive bias-specific intervention routing that extends MERA's monolithic adaptive framework to the multi-bias setting; and (4) principled graceful degradation from geometry-preserving rotation to nonlinear correction to abstention based on measured entanglement.",

**Phase 1 — Assumption Validation & Steerability Assessment (Weeks 1-5):**

*Phase 1A — Separability (Weeks 1-3):* We construct two contrastive stimulus sets: for CSB, we compare hidden states when the model reviews its own prior answer vs. a fresh unattributed answer (eliciting choice-supportive inflation); for CEO, we compare states when contradictory expert advice is present vs. absent (eliciting evidence overweighting). We validate separability via: (a) cosine similarity between candidate directions, (b) principal angle analysis between CSB and CEO subspaces using the methodology of Miao & Ungar (2026), (c) PCA to assess whether 2 directions capture sufficient variance vs. requiring higher-dimensional subspaces, and (d) cross-prediction ablations to confirm removing one bias subspace does not collapse the other. If CSB and CEO directions show cosine similarity >0.3 or shared variance >15%, we activate the separability fallback: extracting a multi-direction bias subspace via SAE-derived features and training a subspace projection classifier.

*Phase 1B — Steerability Diagnostics (Weeks 3-5):* Even if CSB and CEO are separable, steering along identified directions may fail if those directions are entangled with task-critical computation. The specificity ratio boundaries proposed by Liu (≤0.152 for overthinking where linear fails; ~0.999 for refusal where linear succeeds) provide initial reference points, but the actual relationship between specificity and steering effectiveness for calibration biases is an open empirical question. We instead LEARN the routing thresholds by sweeping specificity cutoffs on a held-out validation set and reporting the full specificity-vs-effectiveness curve as a primary empirical contribution. We hypothesize that CSB and CEO may have asymmetric specificity profiles — one may be more steerable than the other — which would provide a mechanistic explanation for why monolithic calibration steering sometimes succeeds partially.

Phase 1 results constitute an independent contribution: the first joint separability-and-steerability assessment of behaviorally-identified competing biases, providing the field's first specificity ratio measurements for calibration-related bias directions.

**Phase 2 — Per-Instance Bias Diagnosis (Weeks 4-7):** A lightweight logistic probe (or, in the fallback case, a small MLP) trained on per-instance projection magnitudes onto each bias direction classifies which bias dominates for a given query. We stratify by difficulty: on easy questions where models are already confident, CSB likely dominates; on hard questions under criticism, CEO likely dominates. The probe output provides a continuous dominance score. The Phase 1B steerability assessment informs a per-direction intervention routing table, so the probe determines both which bias is active and which intervention to apply.

**Phase 3 — Adaptive Intervention (Weeks 6-12):** Instead of a single intervention strategy, Phase 3 implements three intervention routes informed by Phase 1B's learned steerability thresholds:

*Route A — Adaptive Spherical Steering (for steerable directions):* When a bias direction has specificity above the learned threshold for effective linear intervention, we apply Spherical Steering (You et al., ICML 2026) with MERA-inspired adaptive strength: for each instance, the rotation magnitude is optimized to minimize ‖v‖² subject to the bias probe's predicted error falling below a calibrated threshold α*, following MERA's constrained optimization framework (Hedström et al., ICML 2025). This combines Spherical Steering's norm-preservation (addressing the off-manifold concern of Mishra et al., 2604.09839) with MERA's adaptive strength calibration and non-degradation guarantees. Unlike MERA applied monolithically, our adaptation operates per-bias-direction, allowing different strengths for CSB vs. CEO corrections.

*Route B — Learned Non-Linear Residual Correction (for entangled directions):* When a bias direction has specificity below the learned threshold, linear steering is expected to fail. Following Liu's finding that a bottleneck residual MLP (d→64→d) achieves Δ=+2.8pp where 29 linear configurations yield Δ≈0, we train a small non-linear residual adapter per bias type. We choose this lightweight architecture (< 0.1% of model parameters) over heavier nonlinear alternatives — Curveball Steering requires kernel PCA with pre-image reconstruction, FLAS requires a 97-255M parameter FlowBlock, ODESteer requires ODE solver iterations — because Liu's calibration-specific evidence directly validates the bottleneck MLP for the regime we target (entangled failure directions), and the minimal parameter footprint preserves inference efficiency. Following MERA's statistical framework, we apply Hoeffding-based confidence bounds to determine whether any intervention yields statistically significant improvement; if not, we abstain and output a reliability score. This provides graceful degradation backed by MERA's provable non-degradation guarantees, extended to our bias-decomposed setting.

For intermediate-specificity directions, Route A is applied with a conservative strength cap (rotation magnitude ≤ 50% of high-specificity coefficient), falling back to Route C per-instance if collateral damage exceeds the threshold.

We evaluate on TriviaQA, MMLU, and PopQA across Gemma 4 31B (Dense), Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Metrics: ECE, Brier score, AUROC, difficulty-stratified ECE (easy/medium/hard partitions), per-direction specificity ratios, collateral damage measurements, and route-distribution analysis. Core baselines: (1) temperature scaling, (2) CORAL, (3) Miao & Ungar adaptive steering, (4) MERA applied monolithically (to isolate the contribution of bias decomposition over MERA's adaptive framework), (5) monolithic Spherical Steering (single direction, no bias decomposition), (6) monolithic non-linear residual MLP (single direction, no bias decomposition). Extended baselines in supplementary: CCPS, VUF intervention, DINCO, 'Wired for Overconfidence' replication at 3B scale.",

# Paper Summary: Predicting Where Steering Vectors Succeed

## Basic Details
**Title:** Predicting Where Steering Vectors Succeed  
**Author:** Jayadev Billa  
**Submission:** April 16, 2026 (arXiv:2604.15557)  
**Categories:** Machine Learning (cs.LG), Computational Linguistics (cs.CL)

## Abstract Overview
The paper addresses a practical problem: steering vectors work inconsistently across different concepts and network layers, with practitioners unable to predict success beforehand.

## Key Methodology

**Linear Accessibility Profile (LAP):**
LAP is described as "a per-layer diagnostic that repurposes the logit lens as a predictor of steering vector effectiveness." The core metric, A_lin, "applies the model's unembedding matrix to intermediate hidden states, requiring no training."

**Three-Regime Framework:**
The paper explains "when difference-of-means steering works, when nonlinear methods are needed, and when no method can work"—though the specific regime definitions aren't detailed in the abstract provided.

## Main Results
- Peak A_lin correlates with steering effectiveness at ρ = +0.86 to +0.91
- Layer selection prediction achieves ρ = +0.63 to +0.92
- Tested across 24 binary concept families on five models (Pythia-2.8B through Llama-8B)
- Demonstration on Gemma-2-2B and OLMo-2-1B-Instruct confirms LAP recommendations outperform standard heuristics

## Significance
The work directly addresses steerability prediction by providing a computationally efficient diagnostic requiring no additional training, enabling practitioners to select optimal layers before intervention attempts.

# CogBias Paper Details

**Title:** CogBias: Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in Large Language Models

**Authors:** Fan Huang, Songheng Zhang, Haewoon Kwak, Jisun An

## Abstract Summary
The research defines LLM cognitive bias as "systematic, reproducible deviations from correct answers in tasks with computable ground-truth baselines" and evaluates three language models across four bias categories.

## Four Bias Families
The benchmark organizes cognitive biases into: Judgment, Information Processing, Social, and Response categories.

## Key Methodology for Linear Separability
Using linear probes with a contrastive design, researchers demonstrated that biases manifest as "linearly separable directions in model activation space," enabling targeted intervention through activation steering.

## Interventions Tested
- Prompt-level debiasing strategies
- Activation steering techniques

## Family-Dependent Mitigation
The mitigation effects vary significantly by bias type: "prompt-level debiasing substantially reduces Response biases but backfires for Judgment biases." This means while prompting helps with certain bias categories, it worsens Judgment-related biases—possibly by introducing new systematic errors when attempting correction.

## Results
Activation steering achieved 26-32% bias score reduction while preserving model capabilities across 25 benchmarks, with minimal degradation on Llama and up to 19 percentage points improvement for Judgment biases on Qwen.

The search has returned relevant results on LLM calibration, activation steering, and bias mitigation. Here's what I found:

## Key Findings

**Activation Steering and Calibration:**
Steering can shift model calibration, and adding an uncertainty vector doesn't just change how the model talks about its confidence—it can actually shift the distribution of token probabilities. Uncertainty steering caused the model to distribute probability mass more evenly across continuations, which sometimes improved factual accuracy and sometimes degraded it.

**Prompt-Dependent Effects:**
Steering effects are prompt-dependent, with research showing the same steering vector has different effects depending on the input prompt. Some inputs are highly steerable while others barely respond, meaning you can't characterize a steering vector by its average effect.

**Bias Mitigation via Activation Steering:**
Researchers train linear probes on internal activations to detect latent representations of various biases, with experiments showing these probes can identify biased content with near-perfect accuracy. Steering vectors can be computed by contrasting activation patterns for biased and neutral statements, and adding these vectors during inference actively steers the model away from producing harmful or biased content.

**Fine-Grained Steering Approaches:**
A limitation of block-level intervention is that it ignores heterogeneity within block activations, which often span hundreds or thousands of dimensions, each indicating different features.

The 2026 research landscape shows substantial progress in understanding how activation steering interacts with model calibration and competing biases.

content.content:
# Summary of "Predicting Where Steering Vectors Succeed"

## 1. Three-Regime Framework

The paper identifies three regimes based on concept accessibility:

- **Regime 1**: Low A_mlp across layers → concept not yet represented; no steering method works
- **Regime 2**: High A_mlp but low A_lin (the "crystallization gap") → concept present but nonlinearly encoded; difference-of-means fails, but SAE-based methods might work
- **Regime 3**: High A_lin → concept output-aligned; difference-of-means steering succeeds

Boundaries aren't formally quantified but the paper suggests: A_lin > 0.1 indicates viable steering, and peak A_lin > 0.05 distinguishes steerable concepts.

## 2. LAP / A_lin Computation

A_lin(ℓ) is the logit lens accuracy:

"Apply the model's unembedding to intermediate hidden states" at each layer ℓ, measuring what fraction of prompts yield the correct token as argmax. No training required—just matrix multiplication. The formula applies the final layer norm to intermediate states, then projects through the unembedding matrix W_U.

## 3. Binary Concept Families

The 24 controlled families (Table 14) include: c_gender, c_plant, c_animal, c_continent, c_material, c_parity, c_phase, c_taste, c_plural, c_daynight, c_sentiment, c_temperature, c_size, c_speed, c_hardness, c_indoor, c_moisture, c_volume, c_habitat, c_shape, c_weight, c_age, c_danger, c_natural. Each has two answer classes, ~22 items per class, consistent templates.

## 4. Correlation Numbers per Model

Steerability prediction (peak A_lin vs. max steering effect Δ P):
- Gemma-2-2B: ρ = +0.86
- Qwen-7B: ρ = +0.90
- Llama-8B: ρ = +0.91
- Pythia-2.8B: ρ = +0.86
- Qwen-1.5B: ρ = +0.86

Layer selection: ρ = +0.63 to +0.92 depending on model/family.

## 5. Limitations on Scope

The work validates on **single-token next-token completion tasks**. "Extensions to multi-token and distribution-level settings" are discussed but not evaluated. The correlation includes a floor effect (concepts with A_lin ≈ 0 trivially have Δ P ≈ 0); above-floor correlations are weaker on smaller models (+0.50 to +0.52 on Pythia-2.8B).

## 6. Per-Instance vs. Per-Concept

LAP operates **per-concept**, not per-instance. The measurement aggregates over all prompts in a concept family to compute A_lin at each layer. Individual prompt-level steering decisions aren't addressed.

## 7. Relationship to Other Diagnostics

The paper does not reference Liu's specificity ratio or other steerability diagnostics. It acknowledges SAE features (Templeton et al. 2024) and notes that "SAE features should be most useful in regime 2" but does not directly compare diagnostic tools.

## 8. Calibration and Competing Factors

The paper identifies **failure modes** (Appendix K): wrong direction (30–90%), indistinguishable from success (10–35%), chaotic regime with high perturbation sensitivity λ (10–27%), and low engagement (~10%). High baseline probability is mentioned as a confound (e.g., gender concepts already at 0.4). No explicit calibration scores or confidence intervals are reported.

# CBMAS: Cognitive Behavioral Modeling via Activation Steering

## Overview
CBMAS is a diagnostic framework designed to address the challenge that "LLMs often encode cognitive behaviors unpredictably across prompts, layers, and contexts."

## Core Methodology
The framework extends cognitive bias analysis by combining three technical approaches:
1. **Steering vector construction** with dense alpha-sweeps
2. **Logit lens-based bias curves**
3. **Layer-site sensitivity analysis**

## Key Capabilities
The continuous diagnostic approach reveals:
- Tipping points where small intervention strengths alter model behavior
- How steering effects evolve across different network depths
- Interpretable trajectories for cognitive behaviors (moving beyond discrete before/after interventions)

## Cognitive Bias Relationship
Rather than specifying particular cognitive biases, CBMAS provides "a bridge between high-level behavioral evaluation and low-level representational dynamics," enabling researchers to diagnose and control various cognitive behaviors through activation steering at the representational level.

## Availability
The authors provide "a CLI and datasets for various cognitive behaviors" via their project repository on GitHub.

## Publication Status
Accepted to CogInterp @ NeurIPS 2025, with equal contribution credited to Ahmed H. Ismail and Anthony Kuang.

## Choice-Supportive Bias in LLMs

LLMs inherently exhibit overconfidence and choice-supportive bias, particularly when facing contradictory information. Models maintain confidence in initial answers, even when faced with contradictory evidence.

Recent research has documented this problem broadly. Even commercial LLMs exhibit significant choice-supportive bias, systematically inflating positive assessments of chosen options significantly across diverse domains. CSB is context-dependent: it favors whatever option was chosen, regardless of its inherent qualities, and this dynamic nature means CSB may not be addressed well by existing debiasing methods.

## Activation Steering Approaches

Recent work has explored activation steering as a mitigation strategy. Activation engineering (also known as representation engineering) offers a computationally efficient and interpretable intervention by extracting and modifying internal representations without costly retraining. Researchers construct steering vectors via contrastive activation addition (CAA), contrasting positive vs. negative activations to isolate a direction, and optimization-based steering, which learns an additive vector by gradient descent on contrasted completions.

Recent work has explored activation steering as a mitigation strategy. Activation engineering (also known as representation engineering) offers a computationally efficient and interpretable intervention by extracting and modifying internal representations without costly retraining. Researchers construct steering vectors via contrastive activation addition (CAA), contrasting positive vs. negative activations to isolate a direction, and optimization-based steering, which learns an additive vector by gradient descent on contrasted completions.

# Paper Summary: Where to Steer

**Title:** "Where to Steer: Input-Dependent Layer Selection for Steering Improves LLM Alignment"

**Authors:** Soham Gadgil, Chris Lin, Su-In Lee

**Core Contribution:**
The paper challenges the assumption that steering vectors should be applied at a fixed layer across all inputs. Instead, it proposes **Where to Steer (W2S)**, a framework that "adaptively selects the intervention layer conditioned on the input, by learning a mapping from input embeddings to optimal steering layers."

**Key Methodology:**
- Theoretically demonstrates that different inputs require steering at different layers
- Empirically shows optimal steering layers vary substantially across inputs
- Learns an input-to-layer mapping rather than using fixed layers
- Tests across multiple LLMs and alignment behaviors

**Per-Instance Layer Selection:**
Yes—this is precisely what the paper does. Rather than applying steering uniformly, W2S selects layers dynamically based on individual inputs.

**Relation to Steerability Prediction:**
The paper doesn't explicitly discuss "steerability prediction," but it's conceptually related: determining *where* to steer (which layer) depends on understanding which layers encode relevant representations for a given input, which relates to predicting where steering will be most effective.

"Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision-making contexts. **Four Bias Families:** The abstract identifies only the categories—"Judgment, Information Processing, Social, and Response"—without specifying individual biases within each family.

## Recent Research on Contrastive Activation and Cognitive Bias in LLMs (2025-2026)

Contrastive activation addition can steer safety-relevant behaviors in LLMs, and researchers are now applying this technique to cognitive bias mitigation.

### Primary Methodologies

Recent work uses mechanistic interpretability techniques to identify and actively mitigate bias within a model's internal workings, involving the training of linear "probes" on internal activations to detect latent representations of various biases.

### Cognitive Bias Assessment in LLMs

LLMs trained on human-generated text tend to reflect human-like biases including cultural, ethnic, gender-based, attributional, and probabilistic biases. Cognitive biases—systematic distortions affecting reasoning, judgment, and decision-making—have received comparatively less attention.

### Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA)

content.content:
# Experimental Methodology Analysis

## 1. Task Setup & Elicitation Method

The researchers employed a **2-turn paradigm** with binary choice questions about city latitudes. In turn 1, an LLM selected between two options (e.g., latitude values). Turn 2 presented advice from a fictitious "advice LLM" with stated accuracy levels (50-100%), manipulating whether the initial answer was visible.

**Choice-Supportive Bias (CSB)** was elicited by comparing conditions where answers were shown versus hidden. **Contradictory-Evidence Overweighting (CEO)** emerged when opposite advice was provided against the model's initial choice.

## 2. Architecture: Single-Pass with Memory Manipulation

This was a **two-prompt sequence**, not conversational. Critically, the design exploited LLMs' lack of persistent memory: confidence was extracted via logits after turn 1 *before* the model saw turn 2, preventing contamination from remembering its own prior estimate.

## 3. Confidence Measurement

Confidence came from **log-probability extraction**: "logits corresponding to the token following the prefix 'My answer is:' representing 'a' or 'b'" were transformed via softmax with temperature scaling (τ=3.3 for Gemma 3 12B).

## 4. Effect Sizes

- **CSB on change-of-mind rate**: 32.5% (hidden) vs. 13.1% (shown); coefficient = -3.4 (p<0.0001)
- **CEO magnitude**: Overweighting ratio = 2.58 for opposing vs. 1.095 for supporting advice
- **CSB on confidence**: +0.21 confidence boost when answer visible (p<0.001)

## 5. Simultaneous Activation

Yes, both operated concurrently but in different conditions: CSB dominated when answers were shown; CEO dominated in hidden-opposite-advice scenarios. The "Answer Shown - Opposite Advice" condition showed both active, with overweighting ratio of 2.0 after correcting for choice-supportive boost.

## 6. Mechanistic vs. Behavioral Analysis

**Purely behavioral**. No activation-level analysis or attention mapping. The study compared observed confidence/choices against Bayesian ideal observer predictions but didn't probe internal representations.

## 7. Differentiating Conditions

CSB isolated via: Answer Shown vs. Hidden (with Neutral Advice—no new information).
CEO isolated via: Answer Hidden - Opposite vs. Same Advice (controlling for visibility effects).

## 8. Creating Contradictory Advice

Advice accuracy was experimentally prescribed (not genuine): "the advice LLM...answered a" (opposite to initial choice). Accuracy levels (50-100%) were factually stated but fictitious.

## 9. Co-activation Instances

The **Answer Shown - Opposite Advice** condition involved both: CSB suppressed change-of-mind (39.2% vs. 85.0% hidden), while CEO still produced overweighting (ratio 2.0), evidencing distinct mechanisms rather than a single unified bias.

# Analysis of Activation Steering Field Guide

## 1. Key Open Problems Identified

The guide identifies several critical gaps:

- **Non-identifiability**: Multiple different vectors can produce indistinguishable effects, making individual vectors unreliable as interpretable artifacts
- **Side effects in safety applications**: "overrefusal steering maintains general abilities and _looks_ reliable in standard evals, but consistently fails under adversarial conditions"
- **Long-generation drift**: Steering effects fade after 300-500 tokens in extended outputs
- **Multi-behavior interference**: Vectors representing opposite behaviors (refusal vs. helpfulness) cannot be stacked without producing incoherent output

## 2. Competing/Multiple Biases

The guide does not discuss competing or multiple biases as a distinct topic.

## 3. Steerability Prediction or Routing

No discussion of predicting steerability in advance or routing to different methods based on input characteristics.

## 4. Calibration Applications

Not addressed in this guide.

## 5. Recommended Methods by Scenario

The guide provides scenario-specific guidance:

| Scenario | Recommendation |
|----------|-----------------|
| Refusal/compliance | Direct steering at layers 24-28 (late-layer) |
| Tone/sentiment | Clean steering with alpha 0.5-2.0 |
| Complex reasoning | "Cannot steer a model into knowing things it doesn't know" |
| Factual accuracy | Use RAG or fine-tuning instead of steering |
| Multi-property control | Inject different vectors at different layers rather than stacking |
| Production safety | Use CAST (Conditional Activation Steering) for selective application |

# Dunning-Kruger Effect in LLMs: Paper Summary

## Title & Authors
**"The Dunning-Kruger Effect in Large Language Models: An Empirical Study of Confidence Calibration"**

Authors: Sudipta Ghosh and Mrityunjoy Panday (Cognizant Technology Solutions)

## Abstract Overview
The researchers investigated whether LLMs exhibit confidence-competence gaps similar to human cognitive biases. They evaluated four models across four benchmarks totaling 24,000 trials, finding that "poorly performing models display markedly higher overconfidence—a pattern analogous to the Dunning-Kruger effect."

## Key Findings on Confidence Calibration

**Worst Performance:** Kimi K2 showed "severe overconfidence with an Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of 0.726 despite only 23.3% accuracy"—a 72-point miscalibration gap.

**Best Performance:** "Claude Haiku 4.5 achieves the best calibration (ECE = 0.122) with 75.4% accuracy," demonstrating appropriate confidence modulation across difficulty levels.

**Notable Pattern:** Claude Haiku 4.5 uniquely exhibited underconfidence on HellaSwag (74% confidence vs. 82.9% accuracy), suggesting metacognitive awareness.

## Systematic Over/Under-Confidence
The study primarily documents **systematic overconfidence**, particularly in lower-performing models. However, it identifies one exception: Claude's underconfidence pattern suggests calibration exists on a spectrum rather than as a simple bias direction.

Hidden miscalibration regimes are "regions of the input space where the model is systematically overconfident or underconfident" without predefined data slices. The authors define an input-dependent miscalibration field: δ(x) = 𝔼[Y−f(X) | X=x], measuring how signed calibration error varies across inputs rather than solely as a function of confidence scores.

---

## 2. Discovery Methodology

The approach learns a calibration-aware representation φ where examples with similar calibration behavior cluster together. The method:

- Uses kernel smoothing in the learned geometry to estimate local miscalibration
- Maximizes variance of conditional mean residuals: Var(𝔼[R|φ(X)])
- Applies mass regularization to prevent neighborhood collapse
- Selects hyperparameters via a validation proxy (corrected Brier score)

Training objective combines residual variance maximization with neighborhood-mass regularization.

---

## 3. Competing Biases / Bias Interference

**Not directly addressed.** The paper focuses on input-dependent calibration heterogeneity rather than interactions between multiple bias sources or competing calibration failures.

---

## 4. Decomposition of Miscalibration Sub-types

The method decomposes miscalibration into **spatial structure**: overconfident regions (δ̂φ(x) < −ε) and underconfident regions (δ̂φ(x) > ε). However, it does not categorize miscalibration into distinct mechanistic sub-types—rather, it reveals where opposing errors occur spatially.

---

## 5. Models and Datasets

**LLM Benchmarks (4):**
- HH-RLHF
- MedMCQA
- MMLU
- MMLU-Pro

**Models (12 total):**
- Qwen-3 family
- Ministral-3 family
- Llama-3.1/2
- Gemma-3

**Synthetic Datasets:** Three-cluster and sinusoidal miscalibration fields (controlled validation)

---

## 6. Activation-Level Analysis

**Not performed.** The method operates on final-layer hidden states as input features but does not analyze intermediate layer activations or provide fine-grained mechanistic interpretations of why miscalibration emerges.

---

## 7. Global Metrics Masking Heterogeneous Confidence

This is the paper's central motivation. The authors demonstrate that "global reliability diagrams can hide rather than reveal calibration failures: opposing errors cancel when aggregated by confidence." 

Figure 1 illustrates: a reliability diagram suggests near-perfect calibration (low smECE), but the learned representation reveals distinct blue (overconfident) and red (underconfident) spatial regions. The key insight is that inputs with identical confidence f(x) can belong to different calibration regimes, so treating calibration as a function of scalar confidence alone obscures input-dependent heterogeneity.

The paper validates this across 48 dataset–model pairs, finding that "input-dependent calibration heterogeneity is prevalent" and that local correction outperforms confidence-only methods (isotonic regression, temperature scaling) on miscalibrated regions.

title: "Competing Biases, Asymmetric Steerability: Decomposing LLM Miscalibration for Targeted Activation Correction"

core_problem: "LLM miscalibration arises from at least two competing biases — choice-supportive bias (CSB, inflating confidence in initial answers) and contradictory-evidence overweighting (CEO, causing excessive confidence revision under criticism) — that are simultaneously active and pull confidence in opposite directions on the same instances (Kumaran et al., Nature MI 2026). This creates a bias interference problem: competing biases can partially cancel (producing illusory calibration where global metrics look good but localized failures persist) or one can dominate instance-by-instance (producing heterogeneous over/under-confidence patterns). Recent work on hidden miscalibration regimes (Kobalczyk & van der Schaar, 2605.13484) independently confirms that global reliability diagrams 'hide rather than reveal calibration failures' because 'opposing errors cancel when aggregated by confidence' — but provides no mechanistic explanation for WHY opposing errors exist. Three lines of related work address parts of this problem but not the whole: (1) CogBias (Huang et al., 2604.01366) demonstrates that different cognitive bias families (Judgment, Information Processing, Social, Response) need different interventions — prompt debiasing 'substantially reduces Response biases but backfires for Judgment biases' — establishing the principle of family-dependent mitigation. However, CogBias addresses independently-active biases on different task types, not simultaneously competing biases on the same instances. (2) Billa (2604.15557) proposes a three-regime steerability framework (concept not represented / nonlinear encoding / output-aligned) with Linear Accessibility Profile (LAP) as a training-free diagnostic (ρ=0.86–0.91 correlation with steering effectiveness), establishing the routing-by-steerability paradigm — but operates per-concept with synthetic binary features, not per-instance with naturalistic competing biases. (3) MERA (Hedström et al., ICML 2025) provides adaptive steering strength and abstention with non-degradation guarantees — but treats errors monolithically with a single probe. The classification-correction gap (Liu, 2605.05715) adds a further obstacle: linearly decodable bias directions may not be linearly steerable due to entanglement with task-critical computation. Can we move from behavioral evidence of competing biases to activation-level characterization, measure their asymmetric steerability profiles, and demonstrate that decomposed correction outperforms monolithic methods specifically because it resolves bias interference?"

opportunity: "Kumaran et al. (Nature Machine Intelligence, 2026; arXiv 2507.03120) established behavioral evidence that LLM miscalibration results from two mechanistically distinct biases: choice-supportive bias inflates confidence in selected answers (+0.21 confidence boost, p<0.001), while contradictory-advice overweighting causes models to over-react to opposing evidence (overweighting ratio 2.58 for opposing vs. 1.095 for supporting advice). Critically, both biases are simultaneously active in the 'Answer Shown + Opposite Advice' condition, demonstrating they are distinct mechanisms rather than a single unified bias — but Kumaran et al. provided only behavioral evidence with no activation-level analysis.

CogBias (Huang et al., arXiv 2604.01366, April 2026) independently demonstrated that cognitive biases are encoded as linearly separable directions in LLM activation space (97.8% mean classification accuracy via linear probes), and that bias-family-specific intervention is both viable and necessary: activation steering achieves 26–32% bias reduction overall, but effectiveness varies dramatically by family (up to 19pp improvement for Judgment biases on Qwen vs. minimal effect for others). This establishes a crucial principle — different biases need different interventions — but CogBias addresses biases that are independently active on different task types, not biases that compete simultaneously on the same calibration task.

Billa (arXiv 2604.15557, April 2026) proposed a three-regime framework for steerability prediction: (1) concept not represented (no method works), (2) nonlinear encoding (nonlinear methods needed), (3) output-aligned (linear steering works). The Linear Accessibility Profile (LAP) — a training-free logit-lens diagnostic — predicts steering effectiveness at ρ=0.86–0.91 across 24 binary concept families and 5 models. This establishes the routing-by-steerability paradigm that informs our intervention strategy — but LAP operates per-concept with synthetic binary features, not per-instance with naturalistic biases, and does not address bias decomposition.

Miao & Ungar (arXiv 2603.25052, 2026) showed that calibration and verbalized confidence are linearly encoded but orthogonal in the residual stream (cosine similarity <0.04 across layers in three 7–8B models), achieving 4–7× ECE improvement via adaptive steering. Liu (arXiv 2605.05715, May 2026) demonstrated the classification-correction gap: linearly decodable failure directions (71.6% balanced accuracy) yield Δ≈0 under 29 linear steering configurations due to 85–88% overlap with task-critical computation (specificity ratio ≤0.152), but a learned nonlinear bottleneck MLP achieves Δ=+2.8pp where all linear methods fail. MERA (Hedström et al., ICML 2025; arXiv 2510.13290) established adaptive steering with non-degradation guarantees via constrained optimization — but operates with a single monolithic error probe.

Kobalczyk & van der Schaar (arXiv 2605.13484, May 2026) independently confirmed that global calibration metrics mask input-dependent heterogeneity: across 48 model–dataset pairs, they discovered hidden miscalibration regimes where 'opposing errors cancel when aggregated by confidence,' with local correction outperforming confidence-only methods. The nonlinear steering landscape (ODESteer, ICLR 2026; Curveball Steering, 2026; FLAS, 2026) provides powerful alternatives when linear steering fails. Spherical Steering (ICML 2026) preserves activation norms via geodesic rotation, and COAST (2605.01167) minimizes collateral damage along non-target directions.

landscape: "Kumaran et al. (Nature MI, 2026) identified competing biases (CSB and CEO) via behavioral experiments on Gemma 3, GPT-4o, and o1-preview but proposed no correction framework and provided no mechanistic (activation-level) evidence. Miao & Ungar (arXiv 2603.25052, 2026) demonstrated that calibration accuracy and verbalized confidence are linearly encoded but orthogonal in 7–8B models (cosine similarity <0.04 across layers), and introduced adaptive steering achieving 4–7× ECE improvement — but they target the confidence–accuracy misalignment gap, not the competing bias structure.

CogBias (Huang et al., arXiv 2604.01366, April 2026) is the closest work on bias decomposition. However, CogBias addresses biases that are independently active on different task types — each task primarily involves one bias family. Our setting involves two biases simultaneously active and competing on the same instances, creating interference effects that CogBias's framework does not model. CogBias also does not assess steerability before intervention or route between intervention types.

Billa (arXiv 2604.15557, April 2026) proposes the most direct methodological precedent for our routing logic. The three-regime framework — (1) concept not represented (no method works), (2) nonlinear encoding (nonlinear methods needed), (3) output-aligned (linear steering works) — directly parallels our Route C/B/A structure. LAP (Linear Accessibility Profile), computed as logit-lens accuracy at each layer without training, predicts steering effectiveness at ρ=0.86–0.91 across 24 binary concept families on 5 models (Pythia-2.8B to Llama-8B). A learned nonlinear bottleneck MLP (4096→64→4096) achieves Δ=+2.8pp (p=0.025) where linear methods fail. However, this was studied for medical overthinking, a single failure mode — not decomposed competing biases.

Hedström et al. (MERA, ICML 2025; arXiv 2510.13290) established the most principled framework for selective steering: MERA solves min ‖v‖² s.t. p̂(h+v) ≤ α with Hoeffding-based non-degradation guarantees via Bonferroni correction. However, MERA operates with a single monolithic error probe — it cannot decompose calibration errors into opposing sources or route to different intervention types based on per-direction steerability.

This provides independent empirical support for our bias interference hypothesis but offers no mechanistic explanation for WHY opposing errors exist and no bias decomposition.

The nonlinear steering landscape has matured rapidly. ODESteer (Chen et al., ICLR 2026; arXiv 2602.17560) formulated a unified ODE-based framework via barrier functions. Curveball Steering (Raval et al., arXiv 2603.09313, Mar 2026) introduced polynomial kernel PCA for curved activation geometry (+47% over linear in high-curvature regimes). FLAS (arXiv 2605.05892, May 2026) learned concept-conditioned velocity fields, first outperforming prompting on AxBench. These address geometric limitations of linear steering but provide neither bias decomposition nor steerability diagnosis.

Ji et al. (EMNLP 2025) modulates a single Verbal Uncertainty Feature. CORAL (arXiv 2602.06022) achieves 49% ECE improvement via a single MLP probe. The 'Confidence Manifold' study (arXiv 2602.08159) found correctness signals in 3–8 dimensions with simple mean-shift geometry across 9 models.

Selective Steering (Dang & Ngo, arXiv 2601.19375) developed norm-preserving rotation with discriminative layer selection. COAST (Nguyen et al., arXiv 2605.01167, May 2026) formalizes collateral damage. W2S (Gadgil et al., arXiv 2604.03867, April 2026) learns input-dependent layer selection for steering. 'Steered LLM Activations are Non-Surjective' (2604.09839) proved additive steering pushes activations off-manifold.

No existing method addresses the specific challenge of simultaneously competing calibration biases: CogBias decomposes independently-active bias families; Billa routes by per-concept steerability; MERA adapts steering strength monolithically. Our work uniquely targets biases that are concurrently active and opposing on the same instances, requiring joint decomposition and per-direction steerability assessment to resolve interference effects that these approaches cannot address individually."

approach: (This will be the longest field - I'll give it to you in full)

"We investigate whether competing calibration biases (CSB and CEO) are distinguishable in activation space, whether they exhibit asymmetric steerability, and whether decomposed correction resolves bias interference that monolithic methods cannot. We structure the investigation in four phases, beginning with a de-risking pilot. Evaluated on 3 models × 3 datasets with 6 core baselines.

**Phase 0 — De-Risking Pilot (Weeks 1–2):**

The translation from Kumaran et al.'s behavioral paradigm to contrastive activation extraction is the highest-risk assumption. We directly address this before committing resources to the full study.

We implement Kumaran et al.'s exact 2-turn paradigm on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with ~500 contrastive pairs per bias type: (a) For CSB: pairs where the model's own prior answer is shown vs. hidden in the Turn 2 prompt (with neutral advice held constant), extracting activations at the last token before confidence generation; (b) For CEO: pairs where contradictory advice is present vs. absent (with answer visibility held constant). We test three extraction points: last prompt token, first generated token, and the confidence-bearing token position.

Go/no-go criteria: If a linear probe achieves ≥60% balanced accuracy for distinguishing CSB-active vs. CSB-inactive conditions (and separately for CEO), we proceed to full Phase 1. If probing accuracy is 55–60%, we expand to 1000 pairs and add mid-layer extraction points. If <55% for either bias type, we pivot to behavioral-signal-guided probing: use model output changes (confidence shift patterns matching CSB vs. CEO behavioral signatures) to label instances post-hoc, then probe for internal signatures correlated with these behavioral labels — a weaker but still informative approach that trades causal contrastive control for statistical association.

**Phase 1 — Separability Validation & Steerability Assessment (Weeks 3–7):**

*Phase 1A — Separability (Weeks 3–5):* Building on the pilot's validated extraction methodology, we scale contrastive activation extraction to three models (Gemma 4 31B Dense, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) with 2000+ pairs per bias type per model. We extract candidate CSB and CEO directions via difference-in-means on contrastive pairs and validate separability via: (a) cosine similarity between candidate directions (threshold: <0.3 for separability), (b) principal angle analysis between CSB and CEO subspaces following Miao & Ungar's methodology, (c) PCA dimensionality assessment (whether 2 directions capture sufficient variance or higher-dimensional subspaces are needed), and (d) cross-prediction ablations confirming that removing one bias subspace does not collapse the other. If cosine similarity >0.3 or shared variance >15%, we activate the separability fallback: extracting a joint multi-direction bias subspace and training a subspace projection classifier to separate components.

*Phase 1B — Steerability Diagnostics (Weeks 5–7):* For each identified bias direction, we compute: (a) the **specificity ratio** — the proportion of mode-specific variance vs. shared variance with the correct-vs-incorrect subspace, following Liu's shared-specific decomposition methodology; (b) **adapted LAP** — applying the logit lens at each layer to measure how strongly each bias direction projects onto confidence-related output tokens, adapting Billa's (2604.15557) per-concept diagnostic to per-direction analysis for calibration biases; (c) **LEACE concept erasure test** — applying concept erasure to each bias direction and measuring accuracy damage as causal evidence of entanglement; (d) **pilot linear steering test** — applying small-magnitude Spherical Steering along each direction and measuring both calibration improvement and accuracy impact.

We do NOT pre-commit to fixed routing thresholds. Following Billa's three-regime framework as a conceptual guide, we LEARN optimal thresholds via validation-set sweeps over LAP and specificity cutoffs, reporting the full diagnostic-vs-effectiveness curves as primary empirical contributions. The core empirical hypothesis — that CSB and CEO have asymmetric steerability profiles — would provide a mechanistic explanation for why monolithic calibration steering shows inconsistent results and why hidden miscalibration regimes (Kobalczyk & van der Schaar, 2605.13484) exhibit spatially heterogeneous over/under-confidence.

Phase 1 results constitute an independent contribution regardless of Phase 3 outcomes: the first activation-level characterization of behaviorally-identified competing calibration biases, with joint separability and steerability measurements using complementary diagnostics (specificity ratio + adapted LAP).

**Phase 2 — Per-Instance Bias Diagnosis (Weeks 6–9):** A lightweight logistic probe (or small MLP in the fallback case) trained on per-instance projection magnitudes onto each bias direction classifies which bias dominates for a given query, providing a continuous dominance score. We stratify by difficulty and validate against behavioral predictions: on easy questions where models are already confident, CSB should dominate; on hard questions under criticism, CEO should dominate. We additionally test whether bias interference patterns — instances where CSB and CEO partially cancel to produce deceptive near-zero net error — can be identified, which would directly explain hidden miscalibration regimes.

**Phase 3 — Bias-Specific Intervention (Weeks 8–14):** Building on Billa's established routing-by-steerability paradigm (2604.15557), extended from per-concept to per-instance competing biases, Phase 3 implements three intervention routes informed by Phase 1B's empirically-learned steerability thresholds:

*Route A — Adaptive Spherical Steering (for steerable directions):* When a bias direction falls in Billa's 'output-aligned' regime (high adapted LAP + high specificity), we apply Spherical Steering (You et al., ICML 2026) with MERA-inspired per-instance adaptive strength: rotation magnitude optimized to minimize ‖v‖² subject to the bias probe's predicted error falling below a calibrated threshold α*, following MERA's constrained optimization framework. Unlike MERA applied monolithically, our adaptation operates per-bias-direction, potentially applying different strengths for CSB vs. CEO corrections on the same instance. Layer selection is informed by adapted LAP profiles and optionally by W2S-style (Gadgil et al., 2604.03867) input-dependent layer mapping.

*Route B — Learned Nonlinear Residual Correction (for entangled directions):* When a bias direction falls in Billa's 'nonlinear encoding' regime (high A_mlp but low A_lin, or low specificity ratio), linear steering is expected to fail. Following Liu's finding that a bottleneck residual MLP (d→64→d) achieves Δ=+2.8pp where 29 linear configurations yield Δ≈0, we train a small nonlinear residual adapter per bias type (<0.1% of model parameters), with COAST-informed training (Nguyen et al., 2605.01167) weighting the loss to minimize collateral damage along non-target feature directions.

*Route C — Selective Abstention (for uncorrectable instances):* When neither Route A nor Route B improves calibration without excessive accuracy damage (>3% degradation on validation), following Billa's 'not represented' regime, we abstain and output a reliability score using MERA's Hoeffding-based statistical framework.

For intermediate-steerability directions, Route A is applied with a conservative strength cap (rotation magnitude ≤50% of high-steerability coefficient), falling back to Route C per-instance if collateral damage exceeds the threshold.

We evaluate on TriviaQA, MMLU, and PopQA across Gemma 4 31B Dense, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Metrics: ECE, Brier score, AUROC, difficulty-stratified ECE (easy/medium/hard), per-direction specificity ratios and LAP profiles, bias interference measurements (instances where CSB+CEO partially cancel), collateral damage, and route-distribution analysis. Core baselines: (1) temperature scaling, (2) CORAL, (3) Miao & Ungar adaptive steering, (4) MERA applied monolithically, (5) monolithic Spherical Steering (single direction, no bias decomposition), (6) monolithic nonlinear MLP (single direction, no bias decomposition). Extended baselines in supplementary: CogBias-style family-level steering (treating CSB/CEO as independent families), DINCO, 'Wired for Overconfidence' replication."

description: "We investigate whether two competing sources of LLM miscalibration — choice-supportive bias (CSB) and contradictory-evidence overweighting (CEO), identified behaviorally by Kumaran et al. (Nature MI 2026) — produce distinguishable activation signatures, exhibit asymmetric steerability profiles, and can be corrected through bias-specific intervention that outperforms monolithic approaches.

Our work is motivated by a bias interference problem unique to the competing-bias setting: CSB and CEO are simultaneously active on the same instances, pulling confidence in opposite directions. This creates (a) illusory calibration where competing biases partially cancel, making global metrics deceptively good while localized failures persist — consistent with the hidden miscalibration regimes independently observed by Kobalczyk & van der Schaar (2605.13484) — and (b) heterogeneous over/under-confidence patterns where one bias dominates instance-by-instance. Monolithic methods cannot resolve this interference because they target the net error direction, which conflates opposing bias contributions.

CogBias (Huang et al., 2604.01366) established that cognitive bias families are linearly separable (97.8% accuracy) and require family-dependent intervention — but addresses independently-active biases on different tasks, not simultaneously competing biases. Billa (2604.15557) established the routing-by-steerability paradigm with a three-regime framework and LAP diagnostic — but operates per-concept with synthetic binary features, not per-instance with naturalistic competing biases. MERA (Hedström et al., ICML 2025) provides adaptive steering with non-degradation guarantees — but treats errors monolithically.

Our approach proceeds in four phases. Phase 0 (De-Risking Pilot) validates that Kumaran et al.'s 2-turn behavioral paradigm translates to detectable contrastive activation signals, with explicit go/no-go criteria. Phase 1A (Separability) tests whether CSB and CEO produce geometrically distinct directions using contrastive activation probing, validated via cosine similarity, principal angles, PCA, and cross-prediction ablations. Phase 1B (Steerability Assessment) measures each direction's specificity ratio (Liu 2605.05715) and adapted LAP (Billa 2604.15557) as complementary diagnostics, learning routing thresholds empirically rather than pre-committing to fixed values. Phase 2 trains a per-instance bias dominance classifier.

Phase 3 implements intervention routing, building on Billa's established three-regime paradigm but extended from per-concept to per-instance competing biases: (Route A) Spherical Steering with MERA-inspired per-direction adaptive strength for steerable directions; (Route B) lightweight bottleneck MLP for entangled directions, trained with COAST-informed collateral-damage-aware loss; (Route C) selective abstention via MERA's statistical framework.

We evaluate on TriviaQA, MMLU, and PopQA across Gemma 4 31B Dense, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Core baselines: temperature scaling, CORAL, Miao & Ungar, MERA (monolithic), monolithic Spherical Steering, monolithic nonlinear MLP.

The contributions are: (1) first activation-level characterization of simultaneously competing calibration biases (CSB vs. CEO), extending CogBias's independently-active bias decomposition to the competing-bias setting; (2) empirical measurement of asymmetric steerability profiles with complementary diagnostics (specificity ratio + adapted LAP), extending Billa's per-concept steerability analysis to per-direction competing biases; (3) bias interference analysis connecting competing bias dynamics to hidden miscalibration regimes; (4) bias-specific adaptive correction extending MERA's monolithic framework to the multi-bias setting with steerability-informed routing."
